Where it began

Abraham Benjamin de Villiers, AB to the cricket world, was born on 17 February 1984 and grew up in Warmbad, the small town known today as Bela-Bela, the youngest of three brothers. He remembered it as an easy-going place where everybody knew everybody. He went to school at Afrikaanse Hoër Seunskool in Pretoria, where one of his classmates was Faf du Plessis, a friend for life and later a South Africa captain too.

After playing for South Africa's Under-19 side, he made his first-class debut for Northerns in 2003–04.

The player

He was 20 when he made his Test debut, against England at Port Elizabeth in November 2004. He opened the batting that day, kept wicket in the next match and saved it with a fifty from number seven, which tells you how his career would go: whatever the side needed.

In 114 Tests between 2004 and 2018 he made 8,765 runs at 50.66, with 22 hundreds and a best of 278 not out. He held 125 catches in the field and another 97 as wicketkeeper. He made 174 to win at Headingley in 2008 and a match-winning hundred at Perth as South Africa chased down 414, their first Test win in Australia for 15 years. In one 2013 Test he took 11 dismissals behind the stumps and made an unbeaten hundred, the first keeper to manage a century and ten dismissals in the same Test. He also captained South Africa in all three formats.

What made him special

People called him Mr 360 because he could score all round the wicket, often with shots nobody else had thought of. In one-day cricket he made the fastest 50, 100 and 150 anyone had managed, the hundred in 31 balls. Yet he could graft too: early on he went 78 Test innings without a duck. In the field he was nicknamed Superman, and his backwards, over-the-shoulder run-out of Simon Katich in 2006 became the stuff of highlight reels.

His bowling was a rarer treat. Two Test wickets in 114 matches suggests the captains had other ideas.

Away from the middle

He was three times the ICC's one-day cricketer of the year, one of Wisden's five Cricketers of the Decade in 2019, and entered the ICC Hall of Fame in 2024. He was a favourite at Royal Challengers Bangalore, who put him in their own Hall of Fame. A keen guitarist and singer, he recorded a pop album in 2010 with his friend Ampie du Preez, and in 2016 he published his autobiography.

And finally

So many stories grew up about his talent at other sports that he set the record straight himself. He was quite good at rugby and golf, he said, and he did not hold any national swimming records. For a man who held so many cricket ones, that seems fair enough.
